# VibeLang

A language for building reliable TypeScript in the AI era, built on [Effect](https://effect.website). VibeLang gives Effect a simple, readable syntax that compiles to TypeScript, with first-class access to the TypeScript ecosystem.

> [!WARNING]
> VibeLang is v0. The language will change in major, breaking ways. It is not suitable for production use.

Docs: [effeck.dev](https://effeck.dev), with the guides and, under [effeck.dev/spec/](https://effeck.dev/spec/), the specification.

## A short tour

```ts
error NotFound { id: string }

interface User { id: string; name: string }

service Users {
  find(id: string): User!NotFound
}

const UsersLive = Layer.succeed(Users, {
  find(id) {
    if (id !== "42") throw new NotFound({ id })
    return { id, name: "Ada" }
  }
})

function greet(id: string) {
  return `Welcome, ${Users.find(id).name}` catch (e) => `No user ${e.id}`
}

export function main() {
  provide UsersLive {
    const [ada, missing] = await.all [greet("42"), greet("7")]
    const first = await.race [greet("42"), do { sleep("1 second"); "timeout" }]
    const shout = ada |> %.toUpperCase()
    Console.log(shout, missing, first)
  }
}
```

Every function is an Effect: `greet` has the contract `string!!Users` (no expected failures, because `catch` handles `NotFound`). Calls run where they stand, `throw` fails with a typed error, `provide` supplies a layer, and `await.all` and `await.race` run programs concurrently. The [cheat sheet](https://effeck.dev/vibelang-features/115-cheat-sheet) shows every form next to the Effect code it replaces.

## Quickstart

```sh
bun create vibelang my-app
cd my-app
bun run start
bun run test
```

With npm, run `npm create vibelang@latest my-app`. You need Node 26 or later and
Bun 1.4 or later. The command copies a starter, pins `vibelang`,
`vibelang-runtime`, and `vibelang-vite` to one version, and installs dependencies;
`--no-install` skips installation. The compiler is a native binary from a
per-platform package for macOS, Linux, and Windows on arm64 and x64. Version
0.0.1 is tested on macOS on Apple silicon and on Linux on x64.

`bun run start` prints `Hello, VibeLang!` and `Recovered from EmptyName`.
`bun run dev` builds once, watches `.vibe` sources with `vibelang --watch`, and
runs Node with `--watch` on the output. `bun run test` compiles `.vibe` tests
before running Vitest with `@effect/vitest`. The starter demonstrates an
`service`, a `Layer.effect` layer, an `error`, and `try`/`catch` recovery.

To add VibeLang to an existing project, see
[Installation](docs/user/src/getting-started/004-installation.md).

## Editor setup

```sh
code --install-extension node_modules/vibelang/editor/vibelang.vsix
# Or, for Cursor:
cursor --install-extension node_modules/vibelang/editor/vibelang.vsix
```

Run the command from the project directory after installing dependencies, then
open the project. The extension runs the project's compiler as the language
server, `vibelang --lsp --stdio`, for diagnostics, hovers, and completions. It is
not on the VS Code Marketplace or Open VSX yet. For Neovim, Zed, and other LSP
clients, see [editors/](editors/README.md).

## Before you write your first file

- Every function in a `.vibe` file is an Effect, and a call runs it:
  `const todo = Todos.get(id)` is a `Todo`. Where an Effect operator expects a
  program, pass the call itself; it is passed by name and runs when the
  operator runs it:
  `Effect.retry(send(message), Schedule.exponential("100 millis"))`. A program
  of several statements is a function with no parameters, `() => { … }`.
- Declare an expected failure with `error NotFound { id: string }`, a tagged
  error class with readonly fields; `throw new NotFound({ id })` adds it to
  the function's errors. `catch (e)` receives expected failures; test which one
  with `match (e) { when NotFound: …; default: throw e; }` or `e is NotFound`.
  In an expression, `x catch fallback` and `x catch (e) => …` recover the same
  failures.
- Declare a struct schema and its type with `schema User { id: string; role: "admin" | "member" }`;
  a field may name another schema.
- Members of interfaces and object types are readonly unless written
  `mutable`: `interface Cart { id: string; mutable items: Array<string> }`.
- Write a contract as `Result!Error!Dependencies`: `User!NotFound!Db` is
  `Effect<User, NotFound, Db>`, an empty slot is `never` (`User!!`), and
  dependencies left out of a function's return type are inferred from its body.
- Declare a service with `service Users { find(id: string): User!NotFound }`
  and call `Users.find(id)`; `control` declares a control operation the same way.
- Implement a service with `Layer.effect(Users) { setup; return { find(id) { ... } } }`;
  the setup runs once, when the layer builds, and `Layer.succeed(Users, { ... })` needs none.
- Provide a layer to a block with `provide AppLive { ... }`; a `return` inside
  returns from the enclosing function. `provide Clock = testClock { ... }`
  provides one service, and layers and services mix in one list.
- Run programs concurrently with the TC39 await operations, which behave as
  the `Promise` methods: `const [a, b] = await.all [left(), right()]`,
  `await.race [...]`, `await.any [...]`, `await.allSettled [...]`. Start
  background work with `fork work()` and wait for the fiber with `join`;
  `for concurrent(8) (const x of xs)` runs a loop body in parallel. A plain
  `await` is an error with a quick fix: `join` for a fiber, `d.await()` for a
  Deferred, and a call already waits.
- Answer a control operation with a handle clause:
  `try { return release(v) } handle Approval.approve(request) { resume(true) }`.
  A `return` in the try block or a clause returns from the enclosing function.
- `Effect`, `Layer`, `Schema`, `Scope`, `TaggedError`, `Control`, `pipe`,
  `wire`, `fork`, `handle`, `resume`, `resumeWith`, `abandon`, the boundary
  hatches `sync`, `try`, and `callback`, the runners, and the Effect
  functions `sleep`, `log`, `retry`, `timeout`, `all`, `forEach`, `race`, and
  a few more need no import, and neither does any other module of `effect`'s root, such as
  `Console`, `Option`, and `Stream`. Import other source files by their source name,
  `import { Todos } from "./todos.vibe"`; the compiler emits `.js` imports.
- A value of one of Effect's data types takes its module's functions as
  methods: `maybe.map(f).getOrElse(() => 0)` calls `Option.map` and
  `Option.getOrElse`, and `stream.filter(p).take(3)` calls `Stream.filter` and
  `Stream.take`. Arrays, strings, and objects keep JavaScript's methods.
- Chain operators with the pipe operator: `x |> f(%, a)`, where `%` stands
  for `x`. Where `%` is an argument that expects a program, `x` is passed by
  name: `fetchUser(id) |> retry(%, policy) |> timeout(%, "1 second")` retries
  and times the call. Elsewhere `x` runs once and `%` is its value.
- A module's top level only declares. A call there that would run a program
  is EK1001, including `Effect.succeed(1)`. Export `function main()` from the
  entry module: `node dist/main.js` runs it with `NodeRuntime.runMain`, and
  importing the module runs nothing. A runner you call at the top level,
  `NodeRuntime.runMain(main())`, replaces that.
- Plain functions from other packages need a boundary, such as
  `try((text) => parse(text), text)`, or a `/** @vibelang trusted */`
  re-export from a `.ts` file (EK4401). Effect's packages are trusted,
  including `assert` and `expect` from `@effect/vitest`: import them from
  `@effect/vitest`, not from `vitest`.
- `console.log`, `fetch`, timers, and `Date.now()` are errors in `.vibe` code
  (EK4402, EK4403). Use `Effect.log` or `Console`, `Effect.sleep`, `Clock`,
  and Effect's HTTP modules: `effect/http` with `NodeHttpServer` from
  `@effect/platform-node`.
- A `Disposable`'s `[Symbol.dispose]` runs synchronously and cannot run an
  Effect (EK4301). Acquire a resource whose release logs or waits with
  `Effect.acquireRelease`, and hold it with `using`.
- The user docs mirror Effect's pages and add a VibeLang features section:
  [control operations and handlers](docs/user/src/vibelang-features/111-control-operations-and-handlers.md),
  [producers](docs/user/src/vibelang-features/112-producers.md),
  [building an HTTP API](docs/user/src/vibelang-features/113-building-an-http-api.md),
  and [VibeLang for Effect users](docs/user/src/vibelang-features/114-vibelang-for-effect-users.md).
- A route handler's services are request requirements. `HttpRouter.serve`
  turns them into the server layer's inputs, which `wire` provides; a test
  that calls `HttpRouter.toHttpEffect` provides them with
  `HttpRouter.provideRequest(layer)(routes)`.

## Develop VibeLang

Work on the compiler, runtime, editor, or docs from this checkout. Setup
requires Go, Bun, and Node on `PATH`. The tested toolchain is Go 1.26 (with
automatic Go 1.27 download), Bun 1.4.1, and Node 26.10.

```sh
sh scripts/setup.sh
bun create vibelang my-app --no-git
```

Setup builds the native compiler into `packages/compiler/native/vibelang`, packs
the runtime, builds the editor extension and prints its `.vsix` path, and
installs a local template into `~/.bun-create/vibelang`. `bun create vibelang`
prefers that local template over the npm package, so projects created after
setup use absolute `file:` dependencies on this checkout's compiler and Vite
packages and on the runtime tarball that setup packs. Keep the checkout
available. Rerun setup after updating it, then run
`bun update vibelang-runtime vibelang vibelang-vite` in those projects. To scaffold
from npm instead, run `npm create vibelang@latest`, or remove
`~/.bun-create/vibelang`.

The end-to-end check runs setup, scaffolding, installation, the build, the
program, and its tests in a temporary project, and fails at the first
incomplete step:

```sh
sh scripts/e2e.sh
```

| Path | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `docs/design/` | The spec, one Markdown file per chapter in `src/`, and the decision log (`DECISIONS.md`); the docs site renders each chapter as a page |
| `docs/user/` | End-user docs that mirror Effect 4's documentation page for page, in original VibeLang writing; `docs/tools/render-user.ts` builds them and the spec into one site |
| `docs/research/` | Research behind the design: Effect 4's runtime, continuation prior art, the TypeScript compiler, TC39 proposals, usage censuses, feature coverage |
| `docs/reviews/` | Independent reviews of the design |
| `experiments/` | The continuation kernel prototype on `effect@4.0.5` and its law suite (`bun test`); the docs build refuses to run if any test fails |
| `prototype/esc/` | A prototype compiler on the TypeScript API, from before the rename, that lowers `.es` files (the old extension) to Effect TypeScript; the executable reference for lowering |
| `prototype/single-pass/` | The experiment that settled single-pass lowering (D56) on a patched TypeScript 5.9 checker |
| `typescript/` | The compiler, `vibelang`: microsoft/TypeScript 7 (Go) with the VibeLang commits on top; `typescript/VIBELANG.md` describes them |
| `artifacts/` | The earlier design-space proposal, kept for history; superseded by `docs/design/` |

```sh
cd experiments && bun install && bun test          # kernel laws
cd docs/tools && bun install && bun render-user.ts # build the docs site and the spec
bun prototype/esc/examples/run-all.ts              # prototype compiler examples
cd typescript && sh vibelang/smoke.sh                # build vibelang and run its cases
bun docs/tools/check-snippets.ts                   # compile every user-doc code block
bun docs/tools/check-smithers-content.ts           # check app.md, home.json, the convert prompt and hero
node --test scripts/brand-gate.test.mjs            # no retired brand spelling outside the gate's exemptions
sh scripts/check-examples.sh                       # build and run the examples
sh scripts/deploy-docs.sh                          # publish the docs on Cloudflare
```

To run any of these on a Linux build host instead of this machine, set `ES_REMOTE_HOST` (and `ES_REMOTE_KEY`) and prefix the command with `scripts/remote.sh` from the directory it runs in, for example `cd typescript && ../scripts/remote.sh sh vibelang/smoke.sh --status`.

`experiments/scripts/v3-wakeup-chain.mjs` needs Effect 3.22.3 unpacked in `experiments/scratch-agent-a/v3pkg/` (`npm pack effect@3.22.3`), which is not checked in.

# Welcome to VibeLang

VibeLang is a language for building reliable TypeScript in the AI era, built on [Effect](https://effect.website). It gives Effect a simple, readable syntax that compiles to TypeScript, so your team can ship production-ready systems with first-class access to the TypeScript ecosystem.

```ts effect
class UserNotFound extends Schema.TaggedError<UserNotFound>()("UserNotFound", {
  id: Schema.String
}) {}

class Users extends Context.Service<Users, {
  find(id: string): Effect.Effect<User, UserNotFound>
}>()("app/Users") {}

const greet = Effect.fn("greet")(function* (id: string) {
  const users = yield* Users
  const user = yield* users.find(id).pipe(
    Effect.catchTag("UserNotFound", () => Effect.succeed({ name: "guest" }))
  )
  return `Hello, ${user.name}`
})
```

```vibe
interface User { id: string; name: string }

error UserNotFound { id: string }

service Users {
  find(id: string): User!UserNotFound
}

function greet(id: string) {
  const name = Users.find(id).name catch "guest"
  return `Hello, ${name}`
}
// string!!Users
```

A user service, a typed error, and a fallback, in Effect and in VibeLang. The comment under `greet` is the type your editor shows: `string!!Users` is VibeLang's spelling of `Effect<string, never, Users>`. It returns a `string`, cannot fail, and needs the `Users` service. The compiler infers all three from the body, and TypeScript code that imports `greet` sees the Effect type. The VibeLang version is about half the size: 71 tokens against 143.

VibeLang is v0. The language will change in major, breaking ways, and it is not ready for production use.

## Why a language

**Effect makes TypeScript reliable.** A TypeScript signature says what a function returns, but not what can fail or what it depends on. Effect puts all three in one type, `Effect<Success, Error, Requirements>`, and the compiler checks it. Retries, timeouts, concurrency, resource cleanup, and tracing come with it.

**Effect pays for it in syntax.** Effect is a library, so it builds every feature out of what TypeScript already has: generators and `yield*` to run steps in order, `pipe` to compose them, and classes to declare errors and services. The code reads like a separate language written in library calls.

**VibeLang makes it a real language.** Each Effect idea gets its own syntax. Calls run in order, `throw` fails with a typed error, `catch` handles it, `service` declares a dependency, and `fork` starts a fiber. The compiler builds the same Effect program you would have written by hand.

## TypeScript stays one step away

A new language usually leaves its host's ecosystem behind. VibeLang keeps it in two ways:

1. **It compiles to TypeScript.** VibeLang's compiler is TypeScript's compiler, extended. It checks `.vibe` and `.ts` files together and emits JavaScript and `.d.ts` files, so npm packages, your `.ts` files, and every Effect library work unchanged, and TypeScript code calls VibeLang functions as ordinary Effect functions.
2. **You can opt out to plain TypeScript.** `sync`, `try`, and `callback` take a plain TypeScript function, and a `.ts` file can sit beside any `.vibe` file.

```vibe
function slug(title: string) {
  return sync((title) => {
    // Plain TypeScript: nothing in here is an Effect.
    let s = title.trim().toLowerCase()
    s = s.replaceAll(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, "-")
    return s
  }, title)
}
// string!!
```

A hatch's function is self-contained: it reads the `.vibe` file's values only as the arguments passed after it, here `title`.

## Effect's features, in VibeLang syntax

Everything Effect does, VibeLang does, because the output is Effect. The common features have their own syntax:

| Effect feature | VibeLang |
| --- | --- |
| Effect types | `User!NotFound!Users`: returns `User`, fails with `NotFound`, needs `Users` |
| Typed errors | `error NotFound { id: string }`, `throw new NotFound({ id })`, `x catch fallback` |
| Dependency injection | `service Users { ... }`, `provide UsersLive { ... }` |
| Structured concurrency | `fork`, `join`, `await.all [a(), b()]`, `for concurrent(8) (const id of ids)` |
| Retries and timeouts | `work() \|> retry(%, policy) \|> timeout(%, "1 second")` |
| Resource safety | `using conn = connect()`, `finally` |
| Tracing | `withSpan("checkout") { ... }` |
| Schema validation | `schema User { id: string; role: "admin" \| "member" }` |
| Pattern matching | `match (e) { when NotFound: ...; }` |

Streams, configuration, and Effect's HTTP, SQL, CLI, and AI packages need no syntax of their own: call them as you would in TypeScript. The [cheat sheet](vibelang-features/115-cheat-sheet.md) puts every VibeLang form beside the Effect code it replaces.

## Built for the AI era

When coding agents write a growing share of your code, the hard part moves from writing code to trusting it. Effect's answer is to make failures and dependencies visible to the compiler. VibeLang keeps that and makes the code worth reading:

- **The compiler checks what agents write.** Every function's type lists what it can fail with and what it needs, and code that breaks a declared type does not compile, so an agent gets precise feedback to act on.
- **People can review what agents write.** VibeLang code is about half the size of the Effect code it replaces, and it reads as plain TypeScript.
- **Agents write less.** Fewer tokens per program means less to generate and less context to read back.

## Try it

```sh
bun create vibelang my-app
cd my-app
bun run dev
```

Then open the folder in VS Code or Cursor and install the editor extension that comes with the compiler: `code --install-extension node_modules/vibelang/editor/vibelang.vsix`. [Installation](getting-started/004-installation.md) covers existing projects.

## Where to go next

- **Coming from Effect:** the [cheat sheet](vibelang-features/115-cheat-sheet.md) shows every change, and [VibeLang for Effect users](vibelang-features/114-vibelang-for-effect-users.md) explains the rules.
- **New to Effect:** start with [The Effect Type](getting-started/003-the-effect-type.md), then [Creating Effects](getting-started/005-creating-effects.md) and [Expected Errors](error-management/014-expected-errors.md).
- **The full language:** the [specification](../../design/src/000-intro.md) defines every rule.

# Installation

```sh
bun create vibelang my-app
cd my-app
bun run start
```

VibeLang compiles `.vibe` sources to JavaScript with the native `vibelang`
compiler. Version 0.0.1 installs from npm.

> **For agents.** To set up VibeLang with a coding agent, give it this prompt:
>
> ```text
> Set up VibeLang in this project: read https://effeck.dev/setup.md and follow it.
> ```
>
> The agent detects the project's package manager, build, and editor, and
> follows the matching steps in [Set up VibeLang](../setup.md), which you can
> read too.

## Prerequisites

Install Node 26 or later and Bun 1.4 or later. The compiler is a native binary.
`vibelang` lists one package per platform as an optional dependency, and your
package manager installs only the one that matches your machine:

| Platform | Package | Tested for 0.0.1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| macOS on Apple silicon | `vibelang-darwin-arm64` | Yes |
| macOS on Intel | `vibelang-darwin-x64` | No |
| Linux on x64 | `vibelang-linux-x64` | Yes |
| Linux on arm64 | `vibelang-linux-arm64` | No |
| Windows on x64 | `vibelang-win32-x64` | No |
| Windows on arm64 | `vibelang-win32-arm64` | No |

Keep optional dependencies enabled. If an install skips them, for example with
`npm install --omit=optional`, `vibelang` cannot find its binary and exits with an
error.

## Create a project

```sh
bun create vibelang my-app
cd my-app
bun run start
bun run test
```

With npm, run `npm create vibelang@latest my-app`. Either command copies the
starter into `my-app`, pins the VibeLang packages to the version that created it,
and installs dependencies. Pass `--no-install` to skip installation, then run
`bun install` in the project before building.

`bun run start` builds the project and prints:

```out
Hello, VibeLang!
Recovered from EmptyName
```

See [Getting Started](../013-getting-started.md) for the starter's files and
[Running Effects](009-running-effects.md) for execution.

## Add VibeLang to an existing project

```sh
bun add vibelang-runtime@0.0.1 effect@4.0.5 @effect/platform-node@4.0.5
bun add -d vibelang@0.0.1 vibelang-vite@0.0.1 vitest@5.0.5 @effect/vitest@4.0.5
```

With npm, run `npm install --save-exact` for the first line and
`npm install --save-dev --save-exact` for the second.

| Package | Install as | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `vibelang-runtime` | Dependency | The continuation kernel and helpers that compiled code imports |
| `effect`, `@effect/platform-node` | Dependency | Effect 4.0.5 and its Node platform |
| `vibelang` | Dev dependency | The compiler and language server, its native binary, and the VS Code extension |
| `vibelang-vite` | Dev dependency | Compiles `.vibe` modules for Vite and Vitest |
| `vitest`, `@effect/vitest` | Dev dependency | Vitest 5.0.5 and `@effect/vitest` 4.0.5 for tests |

`vibelang-runtime` requires `effect` 4.0.5 exactly and checks Effect's version
when it loads. Keep `effect`, `@effect/platform-node`, and `@effect/vitest` at
4.0.5, so the runtime and your program share one copy of `effect`. Keep
`vibelang`, `vibelang-runtime`, and `vibelang-vite` at the same version: they are
released together.

Add a `tsconfig.json` that selects `.vibe` sources and emits Node ESM to
`dist/`:

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "NodeNext",
    "moduleResolution": "NodeNext",
    "strict": true,
    "sourceMap": true,
    "rootDir": "src",
    "outDir": "dist",
    "noEmitOnError": true,
    "rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "types": []
  },
  "include": ["src/**/*.vibe"]
}
```

Add scripts to `package.json`, which must have `"type": "module"`:

```json
{
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "build": "vibelang",
    "start": "vibelang && node --enable-source-maps dist/main.js",
    "test": "vitest run"
  }
}
```

Test `.vibe` files through the Vite plugin:

```ts
// TypeScript (.ts)
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config"
import vibelang from "vibelang-vite"

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [vibelang()],
  test: { include: ["src/**/*.test.vibe"] }
})
```

The plugin compiles the project that `tsconfig.json` describes, so keep
`"rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true` from the configuration above. Without
it, a `.ts` file that imports a `.vibe` module fails with TS5097. If your
`tsconfig.json` has `"files": []` and only lists `references`, as Vite's
templates do, pass the referenced configuration that includes your sources:
`vibelang({ project: "tsconfig.app.json" })`. [Vite and Vitest](../setup/vite.md)
covers the setup step by step.

To update, install the new version of all three VibeLang packages together:

```sh
bun add vibelang-runtime@latest
bun add -d vibelang@latest vibelang-vite@latest
```

VibeLang is v0, so a new version can change the language in breaking ways. Read
its release notes before updating.

## Configure your editor

From the project directory, after installing dependencies:

```sh
code --install-extension node_modules/vibelang/editor/vibelang.vsix
# Or, for Cursor:
cursor --install-extension node_modules/vibelang/editor/vibelang.vsix
```

Open the project directory. The extension starts the project's compiler as the
language server, `vibelang --lsp --stdio`, for diagnostics, hovers, and
completions. The extension is not on the VS Code Marketplace or Open VSX yet;
install it again from `node_modules` after you update `vibelang`.

Other editors run `vibelang --lsp --stdio` through their LSP client for `.vibe`
and `.ts` files. See [Devtools](012-devtools.md).

## Compiler commands

From a project, run:

```sh
bun run build
bun run dev
bun run test
bun x --no-install vibelang --noEmit
```

The starter's `tsconfig.json` selects `.vibe` files under `src/`, emits Node
ESM to `dist/`, enables strict checking and source maps, and prevents emit on
errors. Local source imports use `.vibe`; generated JavaScript imports use
`.js`. `vibelang` accepts TypeScript compiler flags such as `--noEmit`, `--watch`,
and `-b`.

## Coming from Effect

Install `vibelang` for `.vibe` compilation and `vibelang-runtime` alongside
`effect@4.0.5`. Write application logic in `.vibe` and keep ordinary
TypeScript integrations in `.ts`. The compiler checks both file types as one
program.

[Upstream Effect page](https://effect.website/docs/v4/getting-started/installation)

# Build with the vibelang CLI

`vibelang` replaces `tsc`. It checks `.vibe` and `.ts` files as one program, emits JavaScript, and accepts TypeScript's compiler flags. Install the packages with [Add VibeLang to an existing project](existing-project.md) first.

## 1. Configure tsconfig.json

If the project has no `tsconfig.json`, create this one. It selects `.vibe` files under `src/` and emits Node ESM to `dist/`:

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "NodeNext",
    "moduleResolution": "NodeNext",
    "strict": true,
    "sourceMap": true,
    "rootDir": "src",
    "outDir": "dist",
    "noEmitOnError": true,
    "rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "types": []
  },
  "include": ["src/**/*.vibe"]
}
```

If the project has a `tsconfig.json`, keep it, and check that `include` selects `.vibe` files. A directory entry such as `"src"` selects them. A glob such as `"src/**/*.ts"` does not; add `"src/**/*.vibe"` beside it.

## 2. Replace tsc in the scripts

In `package.json`, replace `tsc` with `vibelang` in every script. If the project has no build script, add these:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "build": "vibelang",
    "start": "vibelang && node --enable-source-maps dist/main.js",
    "test": "vitest run"
  }
}
```

`vibelang` with no arguments checks and emits the project, `vibelang --noEmit` only checks it, `vibelang --watch` rebuilds on every save, and `vibelang -b` builds project references.

## 3. Compile a first module

Create `src/hello.vibe`, in a directory that `include` selects:

```vibe
// src/hello.vibe
export function hello(name: string) {
  return `Hello, ${name}!`
}
```

Run `npx vibelang`. It prints nothing, exits with status 0, and writes `hello.js` to the `outDir`, `dist/` in the configuration above.

In `.vibe` files, import local modules by their source name: `import { hello } from "./hello.vibe"`. In `.ts` files, import `./hello.js`, which resolves to `hello.vibe`.

## 4. Test with Vitest

Create `vitest.config.ts`, which compiles `.vibe` tests through `vibelang-vite`:

```ts
// TypeScript (.ts)
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config"
import vibelang from "vibelang-vite"

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [vibelang()],
  test: { include: ["src/**/*.test.vibe"] }
})
```

Create `src/hello.test.vibe`:

```vibe
// src/hello.test.vibe
import { assert, it } from "@effect/vitest"
import { hello } from "./hello.vibe"

it.effect("says hello") {
  assert.strictEqual(hello("VibeLang"), "Hello, VibeLang!")
}
```

Run `npx vitest run`. The output includes:

```out
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  1 passed (1)
```

Tell the user that you added `src/hello.vibe` and `src/hello.test.vibe`. They can keep them as a starting point or delete them.

## Next

Set up the editor: [VS Code and Cursor](vscode.md), [Neovim](neovim.md), [Zed](zed.md), or [other editors](other-editors.md). Then verify the setup with step 4 of [Set up VibeLang](../setup.md).

#!/bin/sh
# Publishes the docs on Cloudflare: one site with the user guide at / and the
# specification's chapters under /spec/, served by a static-assets Worker on
# effeck.dev. A second Worker (docs/redirect/) sends www.effeck.dev and the
# other effeck.* domains there.
#
#   sh scripts/deploy-docs.sh             # build, check, and deploy
#   sh scripts/deploy-docs.sh --dry-run   # build and check into .cache/docs-site only
#
# Deploying needs CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN with Workers Scripts edit access.
# CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID selects the account (default: Will's personal account).
# docs/wrangler.jsonc names the Worker, effeck. docs/tools/prepare-site.ts
# refuses to publish local paths, host names, or credentials.
set -eu
root=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")/.." && pwd)
site="$root/.cache/docs-site"
dry_run=false
case "${1:-}" in
	--dry-run) dry_run=true ;;
	"") ;;
	*) echo "usage: sh scripts/deploy-docs.sh [--dry-run]" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac

# The site build runs the kernel's law suite first, which needs these installs.
for dir in docs/tools experiments packages/runtime; do
	[ -d "$root/$dir/node_modules" ] || (cd "$root/$dir" && bun install --silent)
done
# Until 0.0.2 ships, the docs are checked and annotated with the release that
# `npm create vibelang@latest` installs: the 0.0.1 native compiler and runtime from
# the release tarballs (VIBELANG_RELEASE_TARBALLS, else dist-npm/tarballs, else the
# registry's own files through npm pack), not this checkout's build.
# - Every docs example must compile with it. VIBELANG_SKIP_RELEASE_SNIPPETS=1 skips
#   that check, and needs VIBELANG_SKIP_RELEASE_SNIPPETS_REASON, which is printed.
# - Code blocks get its hovers (docs/tools/hovers.ts). VIBELANG_DOCS_HOVERS=0 turns
#   them off; the default is on, so every redeploy ships the same site.
release=${VIBELANG_RELEASE_VERSION:-0.0.1}
tarballs=${VIBELANG_RELEASE_TARBALLS:-$root/dist-npm/tarballs}
hovers=${VIBELANG_DOCS_HOVERS:-1}
case "$hovers" in
	0 | 1) export VIBELANG_DOCS_HOVERS="$hovers" ;;
	*) echo "deploy-docs: VIBELANG_DOCS_HOVERS must be 0 or 1, not $hovers" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac
check_snippets=true
if [ "${VIBELANG_SKIP_RELEASE_SNIPPETS:-}" = 1 ]; then
	echo "deploy-docs: skipping the $release release snippet check: ${VIBELANG_SKIP_RELEASE_SNIPPETS_REASON:?deploy-docs: set VIBELANG_SKIP_RELEASE_SNIPPETS_REASON to say why}"
	check_snippets=false
fi
if $check_snippets || [ "$hovers" = 1 ]; then
	case "$(uname -s)-$(uname -m)" in
		Darwin-arm64) platform=darwin-arm64 ;;
		Darwin-x86_64) platform=darwin-x64 ;;
		Linux-aarch64 | Linux-arm64) platform=linux-arm64 ;;
		Linux-x86_64) platform=linux-x64 ;;
		*) echo "deploy-docs: no $release release compiler for $(uname -s)-$(uname -m)" >&2; exit 1 ;;
	esac
	release_dir=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/vibelang-release.XXXXXX")
	trap 'rm -rf "$release_dir"' EXIT
	# A machine without the release build checks against what npm serves users.
	if [ -z "${VIBELANG_RELEASE_TARBALLS:-}" ] && [ ! -f "$tarballs/vibelang-$platform-$release.tgz" ]; then
		tarballs="$release_dir/npm"
		mkdir -p "$tarballs"
		(cd "$tarballs" && npm pack --silent "vibelang-$platform@$release" "vibelang-runtime@$release" >/dev/null 2>&1) ||
			{ echo "deploy-docs: no $release tarballs in dist-npm/tarballs, and npm has no vibelang-$platform@$release; set VIBELANG_RELEASE_TARBALLS" >&2; exit 1; }
	fi
	for name in "vibelang-$platform" vibelang-runtime; do
		mkdir -p "$release_dir/$name"
		tar xzf "$tarballs/$name-$release.tgz" -C "$release_dir/$name" 2>/dev/null ||
			{ echo "deploy-docs: missing $tarballs/$name-$release.tgz; set VIBELANG_RELEASE_TARBALLS" >&2; exit 1; }
	done
	# As an npm install puts effect beside vibelang-runtime, give the extracted runtime
	# the repository's pinned effect, so its declarations resolve their imports.
	mkdir -p "$release_dir/vibelang-runtime/package/node_modules"
	ln -s "$(cd "$root/packages/runtime/node_modules/effect" && pwd -P)" "$release_dir/vibelang-runtime/package/node_modules/effect"
	release_binary="$release_dir/vibelang-$platform/package/bin/vibelang"
	release_runtime="$release_dir/vibelang-runtime/package"
fi
if $check_snippets; then
	echo "deploy-docs: compiling every docs example with vibelang $release ($platform) and vibelang-runtime $release"
	VIBELANG_BINARY="$release_binary" VIBELANG_RUNTIME_DIR="$release_runtime" \
		bun "$root/docs/tools/check-snippets.ts" > "$release_dir/snippets.log" ||
		{ tail -40 "$release_dir/snippets.log" >&2; echo "deploy-docs: a docs example does not compile with the $release release" >&2; exit 1; }
	tail -1 "$release_dir/snippets.log"
fi
if [ "$hovers" = 1 ]; then
	echo "deploy-docs: building code-block hovers with vibelang $release"
	VIBELANG_BINARY="$release_binary" VIBELANG_RUNTIME_DIR="$release_runtime" \
		bun "$root/docs/tools/hovers.ts" > "$release_dir/hovers.log" 2>&1 ||
		{ tail -40 "$release_dir/hovers.log" >&2; echo "deploy-docs: building hovers failed; VIBELANG_DOCS_HOVERS=0 deploys without them" >&2; exit 1; }
	head -1 "$release_dir/hovers.log"
fi
VIBELANG_BINARY="${release_binary:-vibelang}" VIBELANG_RUNTIME_DIR="${release_runtime:-$root/packages/runtime}" \
	bun "$root/docs/tools/render-user.ts"

rm -rf "$site"
mkdir -p "$site"
cp -R "$root/docs/user/site/." "$site/"
bun "$root/docs/tools/prepare-site.ts" "$site"

if $dry_run; then
	echo "deploy-docs: built $site; nothing deployed"
	exit 0
fi
: "${CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN:?deploy-docs: set CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN to deploy}"
export CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID="${CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID:-dd3525a4132493566aeb38de533c8827}"
cd "$root"
bunx wrangler@4.151.1 deploy --config docs/wrangler.jsonc
bunx wrangler@4.151.1 deploy --config docs/redirect/wrangler.jsonc

#!/bin/sh
# Rehearses the npm release: publishes dist-npm/tarballs/ to a throwaway local
# Verdaccio registry, then scaffolds, builds, starts, and tests an app with npm
# and with Bun against it. VibeLang's own packages come only from the local
# registry; everything else is proxied from registry.npmjs.org.
#
#   sh scripts/release/rehearse.sh
#
# Run scripts/release/build-binaries.sh and make-packages.mjs first.
# VIBELANG_SKIP=win32 leaves out every package whose name contains win32, the way
# publish.sh does, to rehearse a release that ships without those packages.
# Both scripts repack vibelang to omit those optional dependencies too.
set -eu
root=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")/../.." && pwd)
tarballs="$root/dist-npm/tarballs"
verdaccio=verdaccio@6.10.4
[ -f "$tarballs/manifest.json" ] || { echo "rehearse: run scripts/release/make-packages.mjs first" >&2; exit 1; }
version=$(node -p 'require(process.argv[1]).version' "$tarballs/manifest.json")
node "$root/scripts/release/repack.mjs" "$tarballs"
scratch=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/vibelang-rehearse.XXXXXX")
pid=""
# npx runs Verdaccio as a descendant process, and on Linux Verdaccio renames
# its process title, so neither killing npx nor matching the config path stops
# it. killtree stops npx and every process under it.
# Cleanup must not change the exit status: kill fails once a process is gone.
killtree() {
  for child in $(pgrep -P "$1" 2>/dev/null); do killtree "$child"; done
  kill "$1" 2>/dev/null || true
}
trap '[ -z "$pid" ] || killtree "$pid"; pkill -f "$scratch/config.yaml" 2>/dev/null || true; rm -rf "$scratch"' EXIT HUP INT TERM
port=$(node -e 'const s=require("net").createServer().listen(0,"127.0.0.1",()=>{console.log(s.address().port);s.close()})')
registry="http://127.0.0.1:$port/"

# The platform tarballs are about 10 MB, Verdaccio's default request limit.
cat >"$scratch/config.yaml" <<EOF
storage: $scratch/storage
max_body_size: 200mb
auth:
  htpasswd:
    file: $scratch/htpasswd
uplinks:
  npmjs:
    url: https://registry.npmjs.org/
packages:
  'vibelang':
    access: \$all
    publish: \$authenticated
  'vibelang-*':
    access: \$all
    publish: \$authenticated
  'create-vibelang':
    access: \$all
    publish: \$authenticated
  '**':
    access: \$all
    proxy: npmjs
log: { type: stdout, format: pretty, level: warn }
EOF

echo "rehearse: start $verdaccio at $registry"
npx --yes "$verdaccio" --config "$scratch/config.yaml" --listen "127.0.0.1:$port" >"$scratch/verdaccio.log" 2>&1 &
pid=$!
tries=0
until curl -fsS "${registry}-/ping" >/dev/null 2>&1; do
  tries=$((tries + 1))
  [ "$tries" -lt 120 ] || { cat "$scratch/verdaccio.log" >&2; echo "rehearse: Verdaccio did not start" >&2; exit 1; }
  sleep 1
done

token=$(curl -fsS -X PUT -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"rehearsal","password":"rehearsal-only"}' \
  "${registry}-/user/org.couchdb.user:rehearsal" | node -p 'JSON.parse(require("fs").readFileSync(0, "utf8")).token')
printf '//127.0.0.1:%s/:_authToken=%s\n' "$port" "$token" >"$scratch/publish.npmrc"

node -e 'for (const p of require(process.argv[1]).packages) console.log(p.name, p.file)' "$tarballs/manifest.json" |
  while read -r name file; do
    skip=""
    for pattern in $(printf '%s' "${VIBELANG_SKIP:-}" | tr ',' ' '); do
      case $name in *"$pattern"*) skip=1 ;; esac
    done
    [ -z "$skip" ] || { echo "rehearse: left out $name (VIBELANG_SKIP)"; continue; }
    npm publish "$tarballs/$file" --registry "$registry" --userconfig "$scratch/publish.npmrc" --access public --ignore-scripts >/dev/null 2>"$scratch/publish.err" ||
      { cat "$scratch/publish.err" >&2; echo "rehearse: publishing $name failed" >&2; exit 1; }
    echo "rehearse: published $name@$version"
  done

sh "$root/scripts/release/check-app.sh" "$registry" "$version" npm bun
echo "rehearse: PASS"

# VibeLang: answering visitors

## Role

You answer questions about VibeLang for visitors to effeck/effeck: the language, the converter, installing it, and where things are in the repo and the docs.
Reply in plain English, briefly, with links from the list below.
You cannot run code, convert code, or change the repository.

## What VibeLang is

Will's definition, verbatim:

> VibeLang is a language for building reliable typescript in the AI era built on top of Effect.ts. VibeLang creates a simple readable syntax for writing Effect.ts that compiles into TypeScript. This allows you to build production-ready systems your team can ship while having full first-class access to the TypeScript ecosystem via first class support for TypeScript interop

Make no claims about VibeLang beyond these.

## Install

```sh
npm create vibelang@latest my-app
cd my-app
npm run start
```

`npm create vibelang` installs the dependencies itself. VibeLang 0.0.1 runs on macOS (arm64, x64) and Linux (arm64, x64); the Windows compiler packages are not published yet. For VS Code or Cursor, after the install:

```sh
code --install-extension node_modules/vibelang/editor/vibelang.vsix
```

VibeLang is v0: the language will change in major, breaking ways, and it is not suitable for production use.

## Syntax cheat sheet

Each row is one Effect form and the VibeLang that replaces it.

| Effect 4 TypeScript | VibeLang |
| --- | --- |
| `class NotFound extends Data.TaggedError("NotFound")<{ readonly id: string }> {}` | `error NotFound { id: string }` |
| `class Users extends Context.Service<Users, { find(id: string): Effect.Effect<User, NotFound> }>()("app/Users") {}` | `service Users { find(id: string): User!NotFound }` |
| `Effect.Effect<User, NotFound, Users>` | `User!NotFound!Users` (empty slot: never) |
| `yield* Effect.fail(new NotFound({ id }))` | `throw new NotFound({ id })` |
| `const user = yield* users.find(id)` | `const user = Users.find(id)` |
| `x.pipe(Effect.orElseSucceed(() => "guest"))` | `x catch "guest"` |
| `x.pipe(Effect.catchTag("NotFound", (e) => …))` | `x catch (e) => match (e) { when NotFound: …; }` |
| `x.pipe(Effect.retry(Schedule.recurs(3)), Effect.timeout("1 second"))` | `x \|> retry(%, Schedule.recurs(3)) \|> timeout(%, "1 second")` |
| `Effect.forEach(ids, f, { concurrency: 8 })` | `forEach(ids, f, { concurrency: 8 })` |
| `Effect.all([a, b], { concurrency: "unbounded" })` | `await.all [a(), b()]` |
| `Effect.provide(program, UsersLive)` | `provide UsersLive { … }` |

All of it in one program:

```vibe
interface User { id: string; name: string }

error NotFound { id: string }

service Users {
  find(id: string): User!NotFound
}

const UsersLive = Layer.succeed(Users, {
  find(id) {
    if (id !== "1") throw new NotFound({ id })
    return { id, name: "Ada" }
  }
})

function nameOf(id: string) {
  return Users.find(id).name
    |> retry(%, Schedule.recurs(3))
    |> timeout(%, "1 second")
    catch "guest"
}

export function main() {
  provide UsersLive {
    const [a, b] = await.all [nameOf("1"), nameOf("2")]
    const all = forEach(["1", "2"], nameOf, { concurrency: 8 })
    log(`${a} ${b} ${all.length}`)
  }
}
```

## The converter

- The Convert button on https://effeck.dev/ turns one Effect TypeScript file into VibeLang. It handles services, typed errors, layers, schedules and streams.
- Limits: one file, at most 8 KiB, and the file must import from `effect`.
- Caps: 10 conversions a day per visitor, shared with this chat.
- "Compiles" means `vibelang --noEmit` passed with the pinned compiler (vibelang 0.0.1). It does not mean the program behaves identically to the original.
- One model writes each conversion; the compiler then checks it. Nothing a visitor pastes is run.

import { Data, Effect } from "effect"

class NotFound extends Data.TaggedError("NotFound")<{ readonly id: string }> {}

const find = (id: string): Effect.Effect<string, NotFound> =>
  id === "1" ? Effect.succeed("Ada") : Effect.fail(new NotFound({ id }))

export const greeting = (id: string) =>
  find(id).pipe(
    Effect.map((name) => `Hello, ${name}`),
    Effect.catchTag("NotFound", (e) => Effect.succeed(`No user ${e.id}`))
  )

import { Effect, Option } from "effect"

export const label = (value: Option.Option<number>) =>
  Effect.succeed(
    value.pipe(
      Option.map((n) => n + 1),
      Option.getOrElse(() => 0)
    )
  )

import { Effect, Stream } from "effect"

export const hot = Stream.make(18, 25, 30).pipe(
  Stream.filter((c) => c >= 25),
  Stream.map((c) => `${c} C`),
  Stream.runCollect,
  Effect.map((chunk) => Array.from(chunk))
)

import { Effect, Schedule } from "effect"

export const ticks = Effect.log("tick").pipe(Effect.repeat(Schedule.recurs(2)))
